en: The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions for the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha’s Resolve to Awaken and the Ten Kings, as Spoken by the Buddha.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Cāngchuān of Cī’ēn Monastery in Mādàshèng, Chengdū.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the city of Kuśinagara, by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River, beneath the twin śāla trees.
At the place where he entered nirvana, he was surrounded by great śrāvakas before and behind him;

an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas had all gathered, and a great assembly of devas and humans—fifty-two classes in total—had come together like clouds, positioned between the first division [of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*] and the *Śāsanāntima-śāsana*.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance that illuminated the realm of Yama and remained in silence.
Then, the Ten Great Kings of King Yama, along with the hosts of jailers, officials, command-giving deities, recording spirits, Yama-messengers, rākṣasas,
and immeasurable varieties of countless classes of ghosts and spirits belonging to his retinue, suddenly surged forth and stood in respectful attendance.
Reverently making offerings and joining his palms toward the Buddha, he then addressed the Dharma King Yama:
"In this Sahā world, all sentient beings have dull faculties and heavy obstructions; they are unfilial toward their parents and do not believe in cause and effect.
Taking their own minds as teachers, they commit the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the ten evil deeds, and consequently all fall into the realm of Yama."
Throughout the dark path of the hells, one is entirely unaware [of its nature]. O World-Honored One, who else but you has given rise to such compassion as in the *Mayūra-jātaka* and other sūtras?

Although a lifespan of a hundred years eventually comes to an end, the eight sufferings of the human realm are like profound pleasure compared to the suffering in the dark paths of hell—the most extreme of all sufferings.
I shall now briefly describe them.
At that time, King Yama, the Dharma King, and the other kings rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni, the Dharma King, being able to employ impartial great kindness and great compassion, has preached for us this illumination of the darkness of the three miserable realms."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Yama and King Qin-guang, saying:

"All sentient beings each possess six consciousnesses, eight consciousnesses, and nine consciousnesses; the meaning of these has been explained previously. Now, within this sutra, there are only two explanations:

the *hun*-consciousness is said to be three, and the *po*-consciousness is said to be seven. Regarding the three kinds of *hun*-consciousness: the first is named the *tai-guang* (womb-light) karmic soul-consciousness; the second is named..."
The subtle essence (*sūkṣma-sāra*), the revolving soul (*paryāya-ātman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three names manifest as the spirit, the soul, and consciousness.

Within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, these open into three: the soul-nature (*ātman-svabhāva*) and the soul-characteristics (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*). They are like waves upon water; though non-dual, they appear dual. As for their nature:

the three bodies (*trikāya*)—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—are the intrinsically enlightened Tathāgata. There is not a single sentient being who does not fully possess these three bodies of the Tathāgata. Thus it is said: "The Tathāgata relies [upon them]."
By means of this wisdom-awareness of mine, I attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree; by means of this principle, I manifested the appearance of parinirvāṇa between the twin trees.
The three *hons* (souls/spirits) follow good and evil karma as they transmigrate through birth and death, experiencing suffering and joy without interruption.

Just as sentient beings today experience the sufferings of the three miserable realms due to the commission of evil karma, so too shall all sentient beings attain the Buddha-way by relying on my cultivation of goodness. All sentient beings!
It is likewise thus: there are seven kinds of *po-śih* (corpse-consciousness), namely: first, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Sparrow-Shade";

second, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Celestial Thief"; third, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Non-Venomous"; fourth, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Corpse-Dirt"; fifth, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Foul Lung";
sixth, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Remover of Impurity"; and seventh, the *po-śen* consciousness of the "Subduing Corpse. These are the seven transformations.

The nature and characteristics of the consciousness-discrimination may be understood by analogy with the *hún* (soul). When all sentient beings approach the end of their lives, King Yama, the Dharma King, dispatches three ghosts:
first, the Ghost Who Seizes the *Hún*; second, the Ghost Who Seizes the Vital Essence (*jīng*); and third, the Ghost Who Binds the *Pò*.
These then bind the three souls beneath the Gatekeeper Tree. This tree is covered in thorns like sharp blades, and two birds dwell upon it.
The first bird is named *Mucalinda*; the second is named *Bamukha*.

In our old village, they have transformed into *kai-lü* birds and utter strange cries, signaling that one should depart for the capital and immediately seek longevity (this bird, according to the local Wu dialect, is said to "cry out when a family's life-force is being split").

In our old village, they have transformed into crows and utter strange cries, saying "A-ho-sa-jia" (this bird, according to the distant Wu dialect, means "sickness comes and the life-force is about to end"). At that time, do you or not know that the deceased has passed away?
The answer is: At that time, they were entirely unaware. The two birds, their wrath blazing intensely, rebuked the deceased, saying:

"While you were among humans, you did not fear the consequences of your karmic offenses; I shall punish your evil. Out of my intent to punish your evil, I will not drink from your brain. While you were among humans, you did not fear the consequences of your karmic offenses; I shall punish your evil.
Out of my intent to punish your evil, I will not eat [your flesh], but shall instead pluck out your eyes and pass them through the gate of the tree to King Yama."

The *Guoku* (Country-Clod) dies; at the southern gate of the *Shāntiān* (Death-Mountain), the deceased person passes through again. Two stalks press against one another, splitting the skull, slicing the flesh from the tiger-patterned body, and disarticulating the bones until the marrow flows out.
Because one dies within the *Shāntiān*, it is called the "Death-Mountain. From here, the deceased enters the Death-Mountain;

on the steep slope, they seek a staff for a path among the rocks, hoping for shoes. Thus, both men and women [prepare] funerary implements; at the head of a three-foot staff, characters are inscribed.
Place the portrait of Kṣitigarbha, along with a set of shoes and the Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for Accomplishing All Requests, beside the *po* spirit (the term for the burial site).

Pass lightly over the deceased as if through a great opening; if there are two stalks [of grass] that do not obstruct the deceased, they will reach the realm of the Dead Heaven across five hundred *yojana* of dark, murky space.
At that time, King Qin Guang addressed the deceased, saying: "Alas! How bitter! A verse of condolence for one suffering in grief says:
'You have departed and crossed the Mountain of Death, Drawing ever closer to King Yama. On this mountain road there is neither food nor clothing;
How can you endure the suffering of hunger and cold?'"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The intermediate state bodies (*antarābhava*) of those who have died within seven days, Are driven toward their fall in numbers as vast as dust;
They are first brought before King Yama for inspection, For they have not yet crossed the ferry of the Nai River."
Summoning the deceased to sit at the gate-bar; at the Gate of Mount Tai, ghosts and spirits assemble to interrogate those who have killed living beings.
Striking their bodies with iron staves so that they cannot offer a defense—this is the first station, King Qin Guang (Acala Vidyārāja).
Second, the Initial River Palace (Śākyamuni Tathāgata):
The burial site is at the bend of the Head River (*Touhe*). Adjacent to the official hall on the bank of the Initial River is the place where one crosses the great river ahead;

this is the Head-Burial Ferry (*Cangtou*), also known as the Ferry for the Deceased (*Wangrenming Naihe*). There are three places where one crosses: first, the mountain water rapids; second, the river.
At the entrance to the bridge spanning the abyss of the three realms of existence, there stands a great tree named the *Yiling* (Clothing-Neck) Tree. Beneath its shadow dwell two ghosts:

the first is named *Duoyi Po* (Robber of Clothes), and the second is named *Xuanyi Weng* (Hanger of Clothes). The female ghost (*Po*) warns against the karma of theft by breaking off both index fingers;
the male ghost (*Weng*), being cruel and unrighteous, seizes the head and feet. Upon first searching, one finds a man carrying a woman on his back, with a bull-headed iron club [held aloft].

Taking the two men by the shoulders, they pursued them across the swift rapids and gathered them all beneath a tree. The *pōguǐ* (Pāpman) stripped off his clothes while the *wēngguǐ* (Vemacitrin) hung them upon a branch;
their transgressions were displayed as they rose and fell before the King of Hell. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
On the fourteenth day, the deceased cross the River of Woes; In thousands of groups and tens of thousands of ranks, they wade through the river waves.
The Ox-Headed King leads the way, staff slung over his shoulder; The Horse-Headed King urges them on, trident held at his waist.
The bitter ox eats the ox as the Ox-Headed King approaches; The bitter horse mounts the horse as the Horse-Headed King abounds.
Bereft of clothing, the suffering of cold oppresses his own body; with evil eyes and bared fangs, the old demon emerges.

Third, at the Imperial Palace of Song (Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva), when a swarm of wicked cats gathers before the official hall on the banks of the two rivers and a great serpent simultaneously appears, one dies.
When people have their breasts cut open and their bodies bound, Yama rebukes the deceased, saying:

"It was not that we lacked compassion that we forced you to commit the karma of sexual misconduct; this suffering is still light—what will it be like when the King of Hell forces you? At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
On the twenty-first day, the deceased becomes increasingly distressed; Only then does he realize the perilous length of the path to the underworld.
Each is called by name to know their destination; In groups they are driven along by the Kings of the Five Officials.
The Fourth Palace of the Kings of the Five Officials (Samantabhadra Bodhisattva).
Between the three rivers, a great official hall was established, with a weighing house on its left and a record-keeping house on its right.

To the left stood a high platform, upon which was a weighing banner; the artisans had constructed it with such ingenuity that seven scales were suspended there to weigh the body and mouth for the seven transgressions.
Those committed through the mental faculty were not weighed, as their gravity was determined by the nature of the intent. Next came...
One should observe the reflection in the mirror upon this scale; there are three distinct categories for marking the eyes:

first, a single mark (one eye) is severed as a grave offense, which is further divided into two—the heavy and the light—corresponding to the offenses of the eight hells; second, two marks (two eyes) are severed as a middling offense, corresponding to the offenses of the hungry ghosts;
third, three marks (three eyes) are severed as a minor offense, corresponding to the offenses of the animals. First, one breaks [the vow of] non-false speech.

After the precepts, while others were committing evil, when they reached the scales, the beam of the scale moved of its own accord, rising and falling naturally. It addressed the deceased person, saying:
"The weight of the sins you have committed is fixed by the scale. The deceased person feigned indignation and said: "I have not yet caused the scale to rise;
why do you act in secret against me? How could I dare not believe this? At that time, Yama took the sinner and placed him upon the scale-pan; the scale-pan [then rose].
As when a deceased person closes their mouth to commit evil and distorts their face, the *Fanglu* (Registrar) descends to conduct an investigation at the *Luoshe* (Record Office).

The officials of the Crimson and Purple Abyss command the weighing and recording of deeds; the *Guanglu Si* (Ministry of Light) seals and stamps the records, compiling the accounts and fully detailing the statutes to be presented to the Palace of Yama.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
The scales of the Five Officials hang suspended in the void; The two attendant boys on either side possess complete mastery over lightness and heaviness.

How could their weighing depend upon the whims of human sentiment? Their rising and falling are determined by one's own past causes and conditions. The two attendant boys spoke this verse: The scales of the Five Officials hang suspended in the void; The two attendant boys on either side possess complete mastery over lightness and heaviness. How could their weighing depend upon the whims of human sentiment? Their rising and falling are determined by one's own past causes and conditions.
The Witness of the Good Youth: At no time does he depart, like a shadow; with ears lowered, he hears all cultivation of goodness and records even the slightest virtue.
The Witness of the Evil Youth: Like an echo following a sound, his essence remains before one's eyes;
he sees the commission of evil and records even the smallest transgression.
The Fifth Realm: The Kingdom of King Yama (Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva).
The Kingdom of King Yama is located five hundred yojanas from the human realm; it is called the Buddhaless World, also known as the Realm of Pretas, and also the Realm of Yamarāja.
The great city is surrounded on all four sides by iron walls, with iron gates opening in the four directions, flanked on both left and right.
On the banner of the donor Gongdang (恭幢), a human head is placed atop; humans can see the human world as clearly as seeing an *āmra* fruit in the palm of their hand.
On the right is the banner of the goddess Kṛṣṇā (Black Darkness), and on the left is the banner of the Lord of Mount Tai. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Among sentient beings, there are co-natal spirits such as Mañjuśrī (魔奴闍耶—a contraction for *Mañjuśrī*) and the spirit on the left who records evil."
One deity has a form like that of a rākṣasa; he constantly follows [the deceased] without departing and records all minor evils. The other deity has a form like that of Śrī (Auspiciousness);
he constantly follows without departing and records even the slightest virtues. Together they are called the "Two Boys.

They record all karmic deeds—whether merit or transgression—from the deceased's previous lives and present them entirely to King Yama, the Dharma King. The King then consults the registers and interrogates the deceased.

Having calculated their deeds according to whether they were evil or good, he divided them accordingly; furthermore, the two banner-leaders reported to that king once more what they had seen regarding human heads.
Next, there were two courtyards: the first was named the Court of King Radiance (*Prabhāsa-rāja*), and the second was named the Court of Good Renown (*Kīrti-śubha*).
Within the central hall of the Court of King Radiance, there was a great mirror-stand upon which hung the mirror of King Radiance, named "Pure" (*Vimala*).
In the past, due to the cause of an unconditioned offering (*anivārita-hetu*), a crystal mirror was manifested as a great royal mirror for King Yama, the Lord of Death.
When this king looks into this mirror, it reflects his own mental activities and all phenomena of the three periods of time, whether sentient or insentient; everything is clearly illuminated.

Furthermore, it is surrounded on all eight sides, with a "mirror of karma" suspended in each direction—a mirror of the collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*) of all sentient beings. At that time, King Yama appears together with them.

The *Sahaja-deva* (Co-born Deity) who keeps the register of beings and the *Puruṣa-śīrṣa* (Human-headed One) see the deceased’s hair-strands; when they cause [the deceased] to see them, they appear immediately before one in the mirror.
All the various karmas performed in this life—whether wholesome merit or unwholesome deeds—each manifest their own forms and images, as if facing a person face-to-face with eyes and ears.
At that time, the Sahaja-deva rises from his seat, joins his palms toward the Buddha, and speaks this verse:
He said:
"The world of Jambudvīpa as I see it now is like a present image in a karma-mirror; there is not the slightest difference between substance and shadow—they share one and the same characteristic."
At that time, the deceased person was seized by terror and agitation in their heart, and spoke in verse:
"I knew beforehand there was the Mirror of Karma; How could I dare to commit sinful deeds? This mirror reflects my body as if it were carved away— How does it know whether one is male or female?"
At that time, King Yama, the Lord of Dharma, again addressed the great assembly:

"By means of the sun and moon of Jambudvīpa, during the tenth-day fasts of the intercalary months of the fifth, ninth, and ninth [lunar] months—specifically directed toward Jambudvīpa—I have distinguished among the human masses those who perform meritorious deeds.
I dispatch overseers of merit and overseers of sacrifices to ride upon white flying horses; in the brief span of a moment, they shall behold the karmic actions performed by those individuals."
He immediately returned and, after a short while, told me what he had seen: "A man who has committed evil deeds was sent to deliver a petition to the Prefectural Governor.
The messenger arrived as described above and commanded me: 'Now, with earnest diligence, you must sever the karma of sentient beings. Yet these beings do not realize this;

they act as they please, committing evil deeds and falling into the three evil realms. It is not that I lack compassion, but for those sentient beings who possess good merit, [I shall ensure they] observe the ten days of fasting."

On the tenth day, maintain the ten precepts and with a sincere heart, advance in mindfulness of Dīpaṃkara Buddha; on the eighth day, with a sincere heart, advance in mindfulness of Bhaisajyaguru Vairocana Tathāgata;
on the fourteenth day, with a sincere heart, advance in mindfulness of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
on the fifteenth day, with a sincere heart, advance in mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha; on the eighteenth day, with a sincere heart, advance in mindfulness of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva.
From dawn until the mealtime, he made offerings and invoked the name [of Amitābha], vowing that he would certainly not suffer the pains of the four evil realms for twenty-three days;

on the twenty-fourth day, he single-mindedly advanced in mindfulness of the Bodhisattva Śrī-mahādevī; on the twenty-fifth day, he single-mindedly advanced in mindfulness of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara;
on the twenty-eighth day, he single-mindedly advanced in mindfulness of the Tathāgata Vairocana; and on the twenty-ninth day, [he continued].
If one single-mindedly and diligently recollects the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja for thirty days, and single-mindedly and diligently recollects Śākyamuni Buddha in this manner for ten such periods,
practicing these observances for one year, one will be able to uphold the ten precepts, be mindful of the ten honored ones,

eliminate pestilence and the five types of disease-demons, attain a lifespan of a hundred years, receive blessings for a hundred autumns, and after the end of life, be reborn in the lands of the various Buddhas.
Furthermore, they are able to make offerings to me, to the *ḍākinī* spirits who seize the life-force,
and to the *vetāla* ghosts that reanimate corpses— namely, those of Caitra (the first month), Śrāvaṇa (the fifth month), and Mārgaśīrṣa (the ninth month)—
on the seven days of both the bright and dark fortnights at the hour of dusk, with such things as incense, flowers, gold, rice, silver coins, silver banners, and silver [vessels].

With worn-out ritual fruits of two kinds (pomegranate and jujube), pure tea, and offerings properly arranged facing north, one should prostrate with single-minded devotion and sincerely recite the Great Divine Mantra one hundred and eight times.

After the King Yama and his retinue have compassionately accepted these offerings, the paper money, banners, worn-out items, and so forth shall all be the appropriate materials for the rite (*jiao*). At that time:

By the power of their original vows, although they were inscribed in the register of death, they were instead entered into the register of life; those who would have met with untimely death or unnatural demise will surely have their lifespans extended.
Those who uphold the precept against frivolous speech will certainly not suffer untimely death or unnatural demise.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke this divine mantra:
Oṃ yamāye dāramarāja ya svāhā.
At that time, having spoken this root mantra, King Yama, the Lord of Dharma, addressed the messenger who oversees merit, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who daily recite this one hundred and eight times, you, together with the immeasurable Yama-rates, shall not leave their side."
It is like guarding one's own eyes; whatever is sought shall be swiftly fulfilled. If there is suffering, it shall be relieved by *agada* (antidote);
if one seeks gardens or wishes for bathing pools, all such various aspirations shall be brought to fulfillment.

At that time, the officials overseeing merit and the rest joined their palms in reverence, advanced to receive the instructions, and withdrew to carry them out accordingly. The seven [realms] are determined according to one’s good or evil karma.
At that time, the Celestial Honored One spoke these verses:
"The five or seven deceased have ceased their clamor; The sinner’s heart harbors resentment, its feelings yet unappeased.
He brushes his hair back and looks up at the karma-mirror, Clearly perceiving all the affairs of his past lives."
Furthermore, it is said that the Courtyard of Renowned Virtue is superior to places where no Buddha resides;

it is established as a distinct Pure Land with ground covered in golden sand and paths layered with silver and jade. On its four sides are built four gates made of the four jewels, and golden trees stand in rows, their branches adorned with the seven treasures and opening forth exquisite flowers.
From every chamber, tiny fruits form; as soon as the flowers bloom, they remain in perpetual spring without fading, and as soon as the fruits form, they ripen.
The fruits grow long and do not fall; within the pond, seven-jeweled lotuses bloom in layers of blue, yellow, red, and white.

On the marshy banks, six kinds of birds warble in harmony with the musical notes of gong, shang, jiao, zhi, and yu. The adornments are so subtle and wondrous that they resemble the Supreme Palace within the Tuṣita Heaven.
Five jeweled seats are established there, which are the place where Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration. In the four directions are seats for the four Great Bodhisattvas.

Those seated there were the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Evil Realms, the Bodhisattva Compassionate Whirlpool of Moisture, the Bodhisattva Vajra-Laughter, and the Bodhisattva Dispeller of the Darkness of Sorrow.
At that time, in a world where no Buddha was present, the Guiding Teacher who transforms beings through compassionate vows, the Bodhisattva Vajra-Earth-Treasury, sat upon the central seat.
Every morning, he entered the *samādhi* of the Ganges sands; having arisen from that meditative absorption, he pervaded the ten directions.

To the sentient beings dwelling in the various kingdoms and their homes, he opens the doors of pure faith by extending both hands with a joyful smile, appearing as the Laughing Sage of Wisdom (also known as the Great Bodhisattva Vajrahāsa). Hearing that their conduct is impure, he pricks his chest with the middle finger of his left hand and departs in tears;
manifesting a compassionate whirlpool of moisture, he enters the hells and causes all others to be freed from suffering.
Through the power of their vows to enter the evil realms and save sentient beings, they remain diligent day after day.

Because they made great vows while on the causal ground in the past, I recall that during incalculable kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Buddha of the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Awakening Flowers (*Bodhimaṇḍala-vyūha-samādhi-vaśavarti-rāja*).
After that World-Honored One entered nirvana, during the period of the Semblance Dharma...
Within that [image] was a Buddha statue; at that time, I conceived great faith and made offerings with reverence for the sake of the noble men and women.
Knowing that my compassionate mother had fallen into hell, I fasted for seven days and prayed with single-minded devotion to save her from that suffering.
On the seventh day, during the fifth watch of the night, the form of a Buddha suddenly appeared within the empty chamber and addressed me.

"Excellent, excellent, O noble son and noble daughter! Those who wish to attain liberation and deliver their compassionate mothers from extreme suffering should resolve upon the unsurpassed, great Bodhicitta.

Because they are able to deliver all parents of the three periods of time, and because they are able to transform sentient beings in Buddha-less worlds and those such as the compassionate mothers in the hells, he is named Kṣitigarbha; he is the treasury for the sentient beings of the hells."
Therefore, in a future age, being capable of rescuing those in extreme suffering, I shall, following the Buddha’s instructions, first give rise to a virtuous mind;
having first generated the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta, I shall act in accord with the conduct and vows of all Buddhas to rescue my mother from her suffering and bring about her liberation.
As that Buddha taught, I thereafter made this aspiration and established this vow, declaring in verse:
If, after I have realized the truth, I am unable to take upon myself the suffering of those in the hells for their sake—unless it can be so taken—I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If, after I have realized the truth, I am unable to provide food to those hungry ghosts for whom it can be provided—I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. If, after I have realized the truth...
If, among the animals, there are those with gnashing teeth who can be saved but are not saved, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If, after I have realized the truth, there are those among the asuras suffering from strife who can be reconciled but are not reconciled, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If, after I have realized the truth, regarding sentient beings for whom I have a karmic connection...
I vow not to attain perfect awakening if I do not enter samādhi.
If, after I have realized the truth, there are those who fear a short lifespan and think of me, vowing not to attain perfect awakening if I do not grant them long life.
If, after I have realized the truth, there are those who suffer from illness and think of me, vowing not to attain perfect awakening if I do not cause their ailments to be healed.
I vow not to attain perfect awakening; If I should realize the truth, yet the King’s malice toward me remains such that he does not grant me pardon, I vow not to attain perfect awakening.
If I should realize the truth, yet I am separated from my enemies and thieves who do not quickly leave me, I vow not to attain perfect awakening.

If, after I have realized the truth, there should be those who, weary of the suffering of poverty, pray to me so that they may not lack abundant food and clothing, I vow not to attain perfect awakening.

If, after I have realized the truth, there should be those who seek official rank and pray to me so that they may not obtain high office, I vow not to attain perfect awakening. If, after I have realized the truth...
If at the time of death you call upon me, yet I do not manifest my form before you, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Once I have realized the truth, for the sake of sentient beings in the six realms, I shall deliver them according to their needs by bestowing the nectar of the Dharma.
Following their various destinies, I shall manifest divided bodies for those whose conditions have ripened.
By means of six kinds of names, [he] shall manifest in body for each successive age.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Kṣatidhvaja, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively.
In a future age, Kṣitigarbha will manifest his body as a condition; I shall bestow upon him a prediction of enlightenment through these six kinds of names. He then spoke in verse:
Anticipating Heaven’s Joy, Kṣitigarbha, Holding a cintāmaṇi in his left hand, His right hand in the mudrā of preaching the Dharma to benefit all devas and humans;
Radiant King, Kṣitigarbha, Holding a khakkhara staff in his left hand, His right hand in the mudrā of granting boons;
Raining down the five grains in abundance; Vajradhvaja, Kṣitigarbha.
Holding a vajra-banner in his left hand and displaying the gesture of fearlessness with his right, he is the Vajradhvaja-karuṇā-akṣayamati-kṣitigarbha who transforms the asuras.
Holding a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) in his left hand and making the gesture of summoning with his right, he benefits the realms of animals;
he is the Ratnavajra-kṣitigarbha holding a precious jewel in his left hand.
With his right hand in the *amṛta-mudrā*, he brings satisfaction to the hungry ghosts;
with his left hand holding the banner of Yama, and his right hand forming the *siddhi-mudrā*, the Vajrapraṇidhāna Kṣitigarbha enters hell to save sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣatigarbha rose up with joyful leaps, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha from before him.
"I have now heard this transmission of the prediction from the Buddha in the void; it is unprecedented.
If in the future I am able to benefit sentient beings in the evil realms and do not abandon this body to become a Great Man," at that time the World-Honored One addressed me, saying:
"Excellent, as you wish! Excellent, as you wish! Immediately the earth shook, and celestial flowers rained down; suddenly, [the body] was transformed.
Having become a Great Man among monks, you shall immediately attain the third fruit of the Mahāyāna. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed me, saying:
"In this world where there is currently no Buddha, you are capable of transforming and enduring [the world]. In a future age, there will be a Buddha named Śākyamuni;
while he dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he will first know of your coming. After his parinirvāṇa, all his disciples shall be entrusted to you. Regarding that *saha*...
The people of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī are fond of evil and do not truly desire the reality you seek; they have never seen one capable of transformation.

If you enter hell to bestow upon them the five or eight precepts, thereby saving lives from the miserable realms—even this single act would surpass the merit of countless bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, I have briefly spoken these verses regarding the merits of your skillful means in future ages.
If there are those who follow their mothers' instructions, they are all the embodiments of Kṣitigarbha;
through the power of his vows, he diligently transforms compassionate mothers with sovereign mastery.

If there are those who remember my name, reciting it a hundred times each day, I shall take upon myself their suffering within the four evil realms and grant them liberation. If there are righteous kings and ministers...
Protected by Śakra, should there be wicked kings and their ministers,
or an ocean of extremely evil offenders punished by Yama for whom no one can provide guidance across— by boarding the vessel of Kṣitigarbha’s vows,
they will certainly reach the other shore.
At that time, after the Buddha of Space had spoken these verses, he suddenly manifested a transformation and vanished from sight.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s prophecy, I, a Great Being, immediately attained the Samādhi of the Well-Manifested Physical Body.
From that time forth, I enter meditative concentration every day to benefit sentient beings, never for a moment becoming weary.
At that time, in the great assembly, King Yama and the other rākṣasas heard the past-life causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Kīrtivatsa;
they deeply believed in cause and effect and his immeasurable merit, and all became his retinue to assist him in guiding others toward the place of goodness.
Having briefly explained these matters concerning his ancient original vows, he concluded.
The sixth transformation becomes the Hall of the King (Maitreya Bodhisattva).
Relying on the two previous kings, the scales and the mirror both manifest: if one is burdened by sin, they reveal evil; if one is encouraged by merit, they exhort toward good.
At that time, the Celestial Honored One spoke this verse:
The deceased lingers on the dark path for six or seven days; One must earnestly fear and alert the mind against folly.
Day by day, look only to the power of merit; Heaven and hell lie within a mere moment.
Seventh: The Hall of King Yama (Bhaiṣajyaguru Tathāgata).
Relying on the judgments and decisions of the three former kings regarding the crime of double-tongued speech, one seeks favorable conditions through both good causes and adverse conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"In the seven-times-seven dark paths of the intermediate state, the subtle body single-mindedly seeks reunion with parents and kinsmen."
At this time, the karmic fruit of merit remains undetermined; one must further observe what causes the deceased has created.
Regarding the lamentations of the deceased’s suffering and grief, the verse says:
"Waiting for the seven-times-seven days, Starved of food and drink, oppressed by cold, The son and daughter [provide] the inherited wealth."
"May you quickly create goodness to support me; If you establish kinship, do not let me enter prison.
My son dwells peacefully at home—what need is there for the suffering of the Yama hells? Even a head ablaze is no metaphor for it.
The Eighth, King Samatā (Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva).

Internally imbued with compassion yet externally manifesting wrathful forms, bestowing both instruction and transformation while meting out punishment—then the Celestial Honored One spoke these verses:
"For a hundred days after death, the deceased remains in further distress; Their bodies are fettered by shackles and chains, and wounded by whips."
May men and women strive to cultivate merit; from this, through wondrous goodness, they shall behold heaven.
Ninth: The Preface to the City of King Duṣprasāha (Akṣobhya Tathāgata), lamenting for the deceased.
Among all the sutras, the Lotus Sutra is supreme; the Dragon Girl emerged from the sea and attained stainless enlightenment.
Among all Buddhas, Amitābha Buddha’s light shines everywhere to eliminate the suffering of heat and cold for those who have passed on;

if men and women desire to rescue deceased relatives, they should today perform the ritual of merit by observing the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*). Through the extraordinary power of this merit, men and women shall not harbor anger, for it can save the deceased from their suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
When a year passes, suffering becomes even more bitter; though men and women cultivate the causes for merit and fortune, their transmigration through the six realms remains unsettled.
By creating scriptures and images of the Buddha, one emerges from the ford of delusion;
yet neither the most extreme evil nor the most extreme goodness finds a place to dwell, while slight evil and slight goodness become guests of the deceased.
Relying on the power of the Buddha’s sutras, the two retributions are determined:
by cultivating merit through pursuit, one ascends to the fifteenth path of the Golden Man, the station of a Wheel-Turning King (Amitābha Buddha).
At that time, the Celestial Honored One spoke this verse:
The final three stages traversed are the mountain passes and fords; Good and evil depend solely upon the causes of one’s meritorious karma.
Even if one does not commit unwholesome deeds, one still fears within a thousand days; For the body is subject to birth from the womb, aging, sickness, death, and untimely demise.
The faults of wrong views and negligence, And the sins of ignorance and lack of wisdom, Are like the revolving of a wheel.
"Constantly dwelling in the three evil paths and the hells," at that time the ten kings,
the various rākṣasas, and the officials of the underworld courts rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, we kings, whether acting through expedient means or in reality, undergo suffering according to our respective natures."
"How can you endure this? Why leave the palace of suffering to return to the home of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the kings, saying:

"In previous lives, when you saw others suffering from evil deeds, you took pleasure in it as your own joy; you encouraged others to commit evil. When you heard of others' goodness, you felt resentment;

when you heard of someone who had attained [the path] and died, you considered it a cause for celebration. You were greedy and stingy with wealth, and through anger you lost all sense of reason. Sentient beings such as these have now attained [this state]."
Regarding those born in the realm of Yama, it was previously explained in detail within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding;
all who possess a mind shall be endowed with this Buddha-nature and shall all attain unsurpassed bodhi.
You who possess a mind should know that the Buddha-nature will certainly cause you to forever leave behind the great suffering of the three fevers. A verse on the Buddha-nature says:
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
I recall that in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, I was then a youth of the Snowy Mountains who first heard this teaching.
Having forever departed from birth and death, I attained the path to Nirvana. At that time, all the kings, hearing these verses of the Buddha, gave rise to profound joy.

Tasting the ambrosial food, they immediately became free from feverish affliction and attained non-retrogression. At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy;
they paid their respects and departed for the place of nirvana, returning to the kingdom of King Yama to believe, accept, and practice it.
Regarding the *Buddha-spoken Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Resolve and the Ten Kings*, the colophon states:
The Tripiṭaka Master Yan Fotiao said, "The Sanskrit original of this sutra was not written in the Tāla script.
Within samādhi, the True Buddha manifested and bestowed this sutra; the Sanskrit text emerged from samādhi and was first transcribed."
After recording this upon bamboo and silk, it was then cultivated and practiced. From North India, it reached the land of China.
The Great Sage Mañjuśrī, within the Hall of Radiance, authorized its circulation. This was during the eleventh month of the tenth year of the Tiānshèng era.

The minor bhikṣu Yuánfú, in order to universally transform the conditions of the faithful and widely open the path for the elimination of transgressions, therefore caused it to be carved into printing blocks for eternal preservation.
For the sake of its circulation, I humbly pray that the Most Honored One, endowed with the ten titles, will bestow his compassion that uproots suffering and grants happiness;

and that the Lords of the Ten Halls of Darkness will graciously record our virtues and grant clemency for our evils, so that the hells may be transformed into pure lands and the boiling cauldrons turned into refreshing coolness.
